### Problem: Pleasant Pairs {#sec-cnt-pidx-pleasant}

::: {.p-statement}
You are given $n$ **distinct** integers $a_1, \ldots, a_n$ with $1 \le a_i \le 2n$. Count the pairs of indices $i < j$ (1-based) with $a_i \cdot a_j = i + j$. There are $t$ test cases.

Samples: $a = [3, 1]$ gives $1$ (the pair $(1,2)$: $3 \cdot 1 = 3 = 1 + 2$); $a = [6, 1, 5]$ gives $1$ (the pair $(2,3)$: $1 \cdot 5 = 5$); $a = [3, 1, 5, 9, 2]$ gives $3$.

Constraints: $1 \le t \le 10^4$, $2 \le n \le 10^5$, $\sum n \le 2 \cdot 10^5$.

Source: [CF 1541B · Pleasant Pairs](https://codeforces.com/problemset/problem/1541/B){.solved rating="1200"}
:::

::: {.p-intuition}
The condition ties a **product of values** to a **sum of indices**, and no rearrangement separates it into "a key of $i$ equals a key of $j$" as in @sec-cnt-pidx-message. What saves us is size: $i + j \le 2n - 1$, so only pairs with $a_i \cdot a_j < 2n$ can ever qualify. Fix $i$; then $j$ must make $i + j$ a multiple of $a_i$, i.e. $j \equiv -i \pmod{a_i}$, so the candidates are $j = a_i - i,\ 2a_i - i,\ 3a_i - i, \ldots$ — about $2n / a_i$ of them. Because the values are **distinct**, $\sum_i 2n/a_i \le 2n(1 + \tfrac12 + \cdots + \tfrac{1}{2n}) = O(n \log n)$: a harmonic sum, the reason the double loop collapses.
:::

::: {.p-approach}
1. **Test every pair.** $O(n^2)$ — $2 \cdot 10^{10}$ pairs for one test with $n = 2 \cdot 10^5$.
2. **Walk the value pairs with a small product.** Keep `pos[v]` (index of value $v$, a direct-address table of size $2n + 1$). For $v = 1, 2, \ldots$ and $w > v$ while $v \cdot w \le 2n - 1$, look up both positions and test $pos[v] + pos[w] = v \cdot w$. $O(n \log n)$ steps by the harmonic bound.
3. **Walk the index candidates.** For each $i$, step $j$ through the residue class $-i \bmod a_i$ above $i$ and test. Same $O(n \log n)$ bound, no table at all.
:::

The buttons are in order. Each one keeps the previous solution and changes only what that form changes.

::: {.panel-tabset .solution-forms}

#### Test every pair

::: {.form-next}
The definition, 1-based. It is the oracle for the other two forms.
:::

::: {.panel-tabset group="lang"}

##### Python

```{python}
def pls_brute(a):
    n, ans = len(a), 0
    for i in range(1, n + 1):
        for j in range(i + 1, n + 1):
            if a[i - 1] * a[j - 1] == i + j:
                ans += 1
    return ans


assert pls_brute([3, 1]) == 1 and pls_brute([6, 1, 5]) == 1
assert pls_brute([3, 1, 5, 9, 2]) == 3
```

##### C++

```cpp
#include <bits/stdc++.h>
using namespace std;
int main() {
    int t;
    scanf("%d", &t);
    while (t--) {
        int n;
        scanf("%d", &n);
        vector<long long> a(n + 1);
        for (int i = 1; i <= n; ++i) scanf("%lld", &a[i]);
        long long ans = 0;
        for (int i = 1; i <= n; ++i)
            for (int j = i + 1; j <= n; ++j)
                if (a[i] * a[j] == i + j) ++ans;
        printf("%lld\n", ans);
    }
}
```
:::

#### Walk the value pairs with a small product

::: {.form-next}
Iterate over **values**, not indices: values are at most $2n$ and distinct, so `pos[v]` is a table, and only value pairs with $v \cdot w \le 2n - 1$ can work. For each $v$ there are at most $(2n-1)/v$ partners, so the walk is harmonic, $O(n \log n)$.
:::

::: {.panel-tabset group="lang"}

##### Python

```{python}
def pls_values(a):
    n = len(a)
    pos = [0] * (2 * n + 1)                    # pos[v] = 1-based index of v, 0 if absent
    for i, v in enumerate(a, start=1):
        pos[v] = i
    ans = 0
    for v in range(1, 2 * n + 1):
        if not pos[v]:
            continue
        w = v + 1
        while v * w <= 2 * n - 1:              # i + j <= 2n - 1
            if pos[w] and pos[v] + pos[w] == v * w:
                ans += 1
            w += 1
    return ans


assert pls_values([3, 1]) == 1 and pls_values([6, 1, 5]) == 1
assert pls_values([3, 1, 5, 9, 2]) == 3
```

##### C++

```cpp
#include <bits/stdc++.h>
using namespace std;
int main() {
    int t;
    scanf("%d", &t);
    while (t--) {
        int n;
        scanf("%d", &n);
        vector<int> pos(2 * n + 1, 0);
        for (int i = 1; i <= n; ++i) { int v; scanf("%d", &v); pos[v] = i; }
        long long ans = 0;
        for (long long v = 1; v <= 2 * n; ++v) {
            if (!pos[v]) continue;
            for (long long w = v + 1; v * w <= 2LL * n - 1; ++w)
                if (pos[w] && pos[v] + pos[w] == v * w) ++ans;
        }
        printf("%lld\n", ans);
    }
}
```
:::

#### Walk the index candidates

::: {.form-next}
Stay on indices but only visit the $j$ that can work: $i + j$ must be a multiple of $a_i$, so $j$ runs through $k a_i - i$ for $k = 1, 2, \ldots$, starting above $i$. The step is $a_i$, so index $i$ costs $O(n / a_i)$ and the distinct values make the total harmonic again.
:::

::: {.panel-tabset group="lang"}

##### Python

```{python}
def pls_step(a):
    n, ans = len(a), 0
    for i in range(1, n + 1):
        ai = a[i - 1]
        j = ai - i                             # smallest j with (i + j) % ai == 0 ...
        while j <= i:
            j += ai                            # ... that lies to the right of i
        while j <= n:
            if ai * a[j - 1] == i + j:
                ans += 1
            j += ai
    return ans


assert pls_step([3, 1]) == 1 and pls_step([6, 1, 5]) == 1
assert pls_step([3, 1, 5, 9, 2]) == 3
for _ in range(300):
    nn = random.randint(2, 12)
    arr = random.sample(range(1, 2 * nn + 1), nn)     # distinct values in [1, 2n]
    assert pls_step(arr) == pls_values(arr) == pls_brute(arr)
```

##### C++

```cpp
#include <bits/stdc++.h>
using namespace std;
int main() {
    int t;
    scanf("%d", &t);
    while (t--) {
        int n;
        scanf("%d", &n);
        vector<long long> a(n + 1);
        for (int i = 1; i <= n; ++i) scanf("%lld", &a[i]);
        long long ans = 0;
        for (long long i = 1; i <= n; ++i) {
            long long j = a[i] - i;
            while (j <= i) j += a[i];          // first candidate right of i
            for (; j <= n; j += a[i])
                if (a[i] * a[j] == i + j) ++ans;
        }
        printf("%lld\n", ans);
    }
}
```
:::

:::

::: {.p-complexity}
**Test every pair**: $O(n^2)$ time, $O(1)$ space. **Walk the value pairs with a small product**: $O(n \log n)$ time — $\sum_{v} (2n-1)/v \le 2n \cdot H_{2n}$, about $2.6 \cdot 10^6$ steps at $n = 10^5$ — and $O(n)$ space for `pos`. **Walk the index candidates**: $O(n \log n)$ time by the same harmonic sum (the skip loop that finds the first candidate runs at most $\lceil 2i/a_i \rceil$ times, also covered by the bound), $O(1)$ extra space.
:::

::: {.p-edge}
- $a_i = 1$: every $j$ is a candidate (step $1$), but only one value can equal $1$, so this costs $O(n)$ once.
- Products overflow 32 bits only if you multiply before bounding: $a_i \cdot a_j$ can reach $4n^2 = 4 \cdot 10^{10}$ in the brute force; form 2 never forms a product above $2n$.
- Distinctness is load-bearing: with $n$ copies of the value $1$ the step loop would be $O(n^2)$.
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistakes"}
- **Starting $j$ at $a_i - i$ without moving it above $i$.** For small $i$ and large $a_i$ the first candidate is fine, but when $a_i - i \le i$ (or negative) you must step up first, otherwise you test $j \le i$ and count pairs twice or index out of range.
- **0-based indices.** The condition uses 1-based positions; with 0-based arrays the test is $a_i a_j = i + j + 2$.
- **Breaking on $a_i \cdot a_j > 2n$ in the pair loop over indices.** Indices are not sorted by value, so that break is wrong there; it is correct only in form 2, where $w$ increases.
:::

**Variants.** @sec-cnt-pidx-message separates the index and value terms into two keys; here they are tied by a product, and the bound on values is what replaces the separation. The harmonic sum $\sum n/v$ is the main tool of the number-theory chapter that follows this one.

- [CF 1520D · Same Differences](https://codeforces.com/problemset/problem/1520/D){rating="1200"} — the separable case: $a_i - i = a_j - j$ is a single key.
- [CF 1462E1 · Close Tuples (easy version)](https://codeforces.com/problemset/problem/1462/E1){rating="1500"} — triples with $\max - \min \le 2$ and values in $[1, n]$: count by value with a table, not by index.
:::
